Overview

htna analyses sequences of events produced by actors of different kinds that take turns: a learner and an AI assistant, a programmer and a coding agent, a student and a tutor. Heterogeneous transition network analysis (HTNA) represents such sequences as one transition network in which each code belongs to one actor type, so the network separates what each actor does after its own moves from how the actors hand over to each other (López-Pernas, Misiejuk & Saqr, 2026). It shows, for example, what the AI does after the learner asks for help, and how the learner responds. Networks can be built for one group or for several cohorts or clusters, compared by permutation or Bayesian tests, and assessed by bootstrap, split-half reliability, case-dropping stability and Markov-order tests; paths and meta-paths of turn-taking can be counted.

The networks are estimated from long event data or clustering results by the Nestimate package and drawn by cograph, with each actor type on its own arc of the layout and in its own colour and shape. The actor partition is kept on the results of every later analysis.

The model

A session is a sequence of codes c1,…,cTc_1, \ldots, c_T, and every code ii belongs to one actor type a(i)a(i). With nijn_{ij} the number of times code ii is directly followed by code jj over all sessions, the relative transition network has the weights wij=nij/∑knikw_{ij} = n_{ij} / \sum_k n_{ik}. The actor partition divides the weight matrix into blocks WABW_{AB} of transitions from codes of actor AA to codes of actor BB: the diagonal blocks describe how an actor continues its own turn and the off-diagonal blocks how the actors hand over to each other. A meta-path is the sequence of actor types that a path of codes passes through, such as Human →\to AI →\to Human.

Installation 

install.packages("htna")

# development version
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("sonsoleslp/htna")

Example

The bundled human_ai data hold 19,347 coded events from 429 sessions in which programmers worked with an AI coding agent, with six human and six AI codes. build_htna() estimates the network; actor_type names the column that assigns each event to its actor.

library(htna)
net <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type")
as.data.frame(summary(net), what = "actor_pairs")
#>   source_actor target_actor n_edges
#> 1        Human        Human      35
#> 2        Human           AI      36
#> 3           AI        Human      36
#> 4           AI           AI      28

All 36 possible transitions between the human and the AI codes occur in both directions. plot_htna() draws each actor’s codes on their own arc.

plot_htna(net)

plot of chunk htna-plot

Meta-paths count the order in which the actors take turns; a lift above one means a pattern occurs more often than the frequencies of the actors would predict.

extract_meta_paths(net, level = "type", length = 3)
#> Meta-paths (type-level) over 429 sequences
#> Rows: 8 | Lengths: 3 | Gaps: 0
#>               schema length gap count n_seq support frequency lift
#>     Human->AI->Human      3   0  3593   402   0.937     0.194 1.41
#>     Human->Human->AI      3   0  3172   422   0.984     0.172 1.25
#>     AI->Human->Human      3   0  2828   403   0.939     0.153 1.11
#>        AI->Human->AI      3   0  2744   383   0.893     0.148 1.36
#>        Human->AI->AI      3   0  2189   403   0.939     0.118 1.09
#>        AI->AI->Human      3   0  2100   397   0.925     0.114 1.04
#>  Human->Human->Human      3   0  1472   396   0.923     0.080 0.46
#>           AI->AI->AI      3   0   392   165   0.385     0.021 0.25

The bootstrap shows which transitions the resampled sessions reproduce.

bootstrap_htna(net, iter = 100, seed = 1)
#>   Edge                   Mean     95% CI          p
#>   -----------------------------------------------
#>   Delegate → Plan      0.609  [0.541, 0.670]  ** 
#>   Refine → Specify     0.412  [0.360, 0.468]  ** 
#>   Ask → Plan           0.411  [0.384, 0.437]  ** 
#>   Check → Execute      0.411  [0.382, 0.444]  ** 
#>   Repair → Execute     0.389  [0.333, 0.454]  ** 
#>   ... and 55 more significant edges
#> 
#> Bootstrap Network  [Transition Network (relative) | directed]
#>   Iterations : 100  |  Nodes : 12
#>   Edges      : 60 significant / 135 total
#>   CI         : 95%  |  Inference: stability  |  CR [0.75, 1.25]

Authors and citation

htna is written by Sonsoles López-Pernas, Kamila Misiejuk and Mohammed Saqr. Sonsoles López-Pernas maintains the package. Questions and bug reports can be submitted through the repository issue tracker. The package citation is available through citation("htna").

The method is described in:

  • López-Pernas, S., Misiejuk, K., & Saqr, M. (2026). How AI-generated feedback hinders or helps learning: A heterogeneous TNA study of learning dynamics. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 42(4), e70285. https://doi.org/10.1002/jcal.70285

Related research:

  • López-Pernas, S., Misiejuk, K., Tikka, S., & Saqr, M. (2026). Role dynamics in student-AI collaboration: A heterogeneous transition network analysis approach. Innovations in Analytics of Learning Dynamics: Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Transition Network Analysis (TNA). https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6082190
  • Rinja, D., Oliveira, E. A., López-Pernas, S., Saqr, M., Specht, M., & Misiejuk, K. (2027). Unpacking vibe coding: Help-seeking processes in student-AI interactions while programming. Proceedings of Artificial Intelligence in Education: 27th International Conference, AIED 2026. Springer Nature Switzerland. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-29763-1_35

Related packages: tna for transition network analysis of single-actor sequences, Nestimate for network estimation and inference, and cograph for network plots.
